title: Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances; Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.3.3-c06, 4.3.3-c03, 4.3.3-c09, 4.3.3-c05. Clues: 4.3.3-c06 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.3-c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.3-c09 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.3-c05 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.3.2-q27, 4.3.3-q01, 4.3.3-q11, 4.3.2-q28, 4.3.3-q02, 4.3.3-q12, 4.3.2-q29, 4.3.3-q03, 4.3.3-q13, 4.3.3-q04, 4.3.3-q14, 4.3.3-q05, 4.3.2-q01, 4.3.2-q11, 4.3.2-q18, 4.3.2-q23, 4.3.2-q30, 4.3.3-q09.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Yield
items.clue: The amount of a product obtained from a reaction.

items.label: Reversible reaction
items.clue: A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants.

items.label: Atom economy (atom utilisation)
items.clue: A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.

items.label: Side reaction
items.clue: A reaction in which some of the reactants react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming a substance other than the desired product.

questions.stem: A solution has a concentration of 20 g/dm³. What does this tell you?

options.text: there is 20 g of solute in each 1 cm³ of solution
there is 20 g of solute, whatever the volume may be
there is 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution
any solution holding 20 g of solute has this concentration

questions.explanation: Concentration measured in g/dm³ is a mass per given volume of solution, here 20 g in each dm³.

questions.stem: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the mass of product collected is almost always less than the calculated amount. What does this shortfall show?

options.text: A few of the atoms are destroyed as the old bonds are broken apart.
Mass is conserved only when a reaction is done in a sealed flask.
The atoms all still exist, but they are not all in the product.
The balanced equation overstates how much product could form.

questions.explanation: Correct: no atoms are gained or lost, so the missing mass is unreacted material, product lost on separation, or atoms built into a different product.

questions.stem: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?

options.text: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful product.
The amount of the predicted product that is collected in practice.
The amount of reactant that has reacted once equilibrium has been set up.
The amount of the energy given out that is transferred usefully.

questions.explanation: Correct: atom economy, or atom utilisation, is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.

questions.stem: A solution has a concentration of 12 g/dm³. What mass of solute is present in 250 cm³ of this solution?
questions.explanation: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³, and mass = concentration x volume = 12 x 0.25 = 3.0 g.

questions.stem: A product is made using a reaction that is reversible. Why does this keep the yield below the maximum theoretical amount?

options.text: The reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is left over.
All of the product turns back into the reactants, and none is left.
Atoms are used up by the backward reaction and cannot be got back.
The backward reaction uses up the catalyst, so the reaction ends.

questions.explanation: Correct: product re-forms reactant as fast as reactant forms product, so the mixture always still contains some reactant.

questions.stem: A student weighs out the reactants, weighs the product she has made and divides one measured mass by the other to find the atom economy. Why is this wrong?

options.text: The mass lost when the product was separated must be subtracted.
The atom economy changes when the reaction is scaled up to industry.
The percentage atom economy is calculated using the balanced equation.
The actual yield of product is needed as well as the theoretical.

questions.explanation: Correct: the specification calculates atom economy from relative formula masses in the balanced equation, so measured masses are never used.

questions.stem: A student needs 7.5 g of a solute. The solution available has a concentration of 25 g/dm³. What volume of the solution should be measured out?

options.text: 300 cm³
0.30 cm³
30 cm³

questions.explanation: volume = mass ÷ concentration = 7.5 ÷ 25 = 0.3 dm³, and 0.3 x 1000 = 300 cm³.

questions.stem: Copper sulfate crystals are filtered from the reaction mixture, washed and dried before being weighed. Which reason for a low yield does this practical show?

options.text: Filtering strips atoms out of the compound, so it now weighs less.
Water driven off during drying shows mass is not conserved.
Washing adds impurities to the crystals and lowers the mass.
Some product stays on the filter paper and inside the glassware.

questions.explanation: Correct: product lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture is never weighed, so the yield falls below the maximum.

questions.stem: In the percentage atom economy calculation, what is the bottom line of the fraction?

options.text: The relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation.
The sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants in the equation.
The relative formula mass of the one reactant that the product comes from.
The total mass of all the reactants weighed out in the experiment.

questions.explanation: Correct: the Mr of the desired product is divided by the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

questions.stem: A student analyses the product mixture and finds an unexpected second compound in it. Which reason for the reduced yield does this point to?

options.text: The reaction is reversible, so some product has changed back again.
Some reactant reacted in a way different to the expected one.
Filtering and washing took some atoms out of the product itself.
The relative formula masses used in the calculation were wrong.

questions.explanation: Correct: a compound that does not appear in the equation shows that some of the reactants took a different reaction pathway.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is made from methane: CH4 + H2O -> 3H2 + CO. Mr: CH4 = 16, H2O = 18, H2 = 2, CO = 28. What is the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen?
What does the percentage yield of a reaction tell you?

options.text: The percentage of the product that has not turned back into reactants.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the mass of the reactants.
The percentage of reactant atoms ending up in the useful product.

questions.explanation: Correct: the amount of product obtained is the yield, and comparing it with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage gives the percentage yield.

questions.stem: A bottle in a laboratory is labelled '0.50 mol of sodium chloride'. What does the '0.50 mol' tell you?

options.text: the chemical amount of sodium chloride present
the mass of the sodium chloride, in grams
the number of sodium ions in the bottle
the volume the sodium chloride fills

questions.explanation: Chemical amounts are measured in moles and mol is the symbol for that unit, so the label states an amount of substance.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. In a sealed container, 4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen. Which statement about the magnesium oxide formed is correct?

options.text: It is less than 8.0 g, as some mass is lost as gas.
It is 4.8 g, since only the magnesium is weighed out.
It is 8.0 g, the total mass of the reactants.
It is 3.2 g, the mass of the oxygen that reacted.

questions.explanation: Mass is conserved in a closed system, so 4.8 g + 3.2 g of reactants give 8.0 g of magnesium oxide.

questions.stem: The masses of the reactants and products in a reaction are known. How are the balancing numbers in the symbol equation found?

options.text: use the ratio of the masses in grams as the numbers
convert each mass to moles, then find the simplest ratio
divide each mass by the first element's relative atomic mass
multiply each mass by its relative formula mass

questions.explanation: Masses in grams are converted to amounts in moles, and those amounts are converted to simple whole number ratios.

questions.stem: In a reaction between two reactants, what is meant by the limiting reactant?

options.text: the reactant that is added in excess
the reactant with the smallest mass used
the reactant that is completely used up
the reactant that is left over at the end

questions.explanation: The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products.

questions.stem: A solution contains 4.0 g of solute in 200 cm³ of solution. Water is added until the volume of the solution is 400 cm³. What happens to the concentration?

options.text: It rises from 20 g/dm³ to 40 g/dm³, as more has been added.
It falls from 20 g/dm³ to 10 g/dm³, as the volume doubles.
It stays at 20 g/dm³, as the mass of solute is fixed.
It falls from 2.0 g/dm³ to 1.0 g/dm³, halving as water goes in.

questions.explanation: The mass of solute stays at 4.0 g while the volume doubles to 0.4 dm³, so 4.0 ÷ 0.4 = 10 g/dm³.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 10 g of calcium carbonate?

options.text: 4 g

questions.explanation: Correct: 10 / 100 = 0.1 mol of CaCO3, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.
